title: Chapter 168: The Patient in Room Three
html:
The Jiujiang Third Psychological Convalescence Centre opened twenty-three years earlier as the city’s first private psychiatric hospital.

Its three sick halls served different markets. The first charged less than public hospitals but offered terrible conditions. The second cost twenty percent above the standard rate and provided dedicated doctors and nurses. The Third Sick Hall accepted only a few patients at several times the price of an ordinary room.

According to the director’s notes, the institution had looked entirely different in its early years. The Third Sick Hall was not originally sealed; it offered the finest environment and commanded the highest fees.

Three months after opening, the center received an unusual patient. The director recorded her arrival in detail, perhaps because that day became the turning point of his life.

A car with out-of-province plates pulled up, and two men helped a heavily pregnant woman from the back seat. The director greeted them personally. After questioning her, he recognized signs of severe mental illness and refused admission out of concern for mother and child.

The man appeared to expect this. He offered ten times the Third Sick Hall’s already exorbitant rate and promised six months’ payment in advance.

The mountain of cash swayed the director and his doctors. Although the first two halls had filled quickly, most rooms in the expensive third building remained vacant; wealthy families generally preferred public institutions.

After pressure from the doctors, the director admitted the woman to Room 3. Once she was settled, the man left a phone number and claimed to be her husband, but he could produce no marriage certificate.

Having accepted the money, the director felt unable to reverse course. The woman was diagnosed with bipolar disorder. She refused to communicate, swung rapidly between tears and rage, smashed whatever she could reach, and sometimes harmed herself. To protect her, the staff stripped Room 3 of every hazard.

Her pregnancy ruled out most medications, leaving counseling as the only treatment. Three months passed, and as her due date approached, the hospital assigned nurses to monitor her around the clock.

Whether through therapy or emerging maternal instinct, her violent episodes subsided. She still avoided human contact but spent hours stroking her stomach and murmuring to herself.

A month later, she gave birth, and her condition improved dramatically. Relieved, the director and doctors called the husband that same day. No one answered.

Alarmed, they hired a private investigator, who discovered that every document the man had provided was false. The staff agreed to contact the police if he failed to return before the prepaid treatment expired. For the woman’s sake, they kept this from her.

Motherhood restored her desire to live, and she began cooperating fully with treatment. She wanted to recover for her child and often asked about her husband, believing he would return once she was well.

Six months passed. The money ran out, and the man had seemingly vanished from the world.

The staff divided into two camps. Some doctors and nurses wanted mother and son transferred, arguing that caring for both without payment created too great a burden. The compassionate director asked for more time, but one of the woman’s nurses accidentally revealed the dispute.

The woman demanded to speak with her husband. An automated message coldly informed her that his number was no longer in service.

The couple seemed to have made some promise before her admission. Its betrayal sent her condition spiraling. She became hostile toward everyone, lost in a dark maze with no exit. Fearing she might harm her son, the doctors removed the baby from her care.

She withdrew completely and refused to communicate. The infant was too young to abandon, and the hospital could not simply adopt him. The staff continued treating her, hoping she would reveal the man’s whereabouts so they could recover the unpaid fees.

No one imagined this arrangement would last three years. The child learned to walk and speak inside a psychiatric hospital.

Those first years form the foundation of a person’s development, when the mind absorbs information at extraordinary speed. He spent them in a warped and complex environment.

With no money remaining, the hospital supported them out of charity. That was tolerable for days, but resentment grew as months passed, until even the staff looked at the child differently.

His mother remained locked in Room 3. Throughout those years, the child constantly begged doctors and nurses to carry him to her door, where he pressed against the viewing window and watched her inside.

After learning to walk, he sometimes wandered there alone and stared up at the door towering over him. Days became weeks, then months. Other children grew among family and friends in colorful worlds; his memories contained mostly whitewashed walls. Inevitably, his behavior diverged from theirs.

Absorbed despite himself, Chen Ge reached the end. The letter read like the director’s private diary.

“This child’s childhood is even sadder than mine.”

He had considered his own childhood among mannequin heads and plastic bones unfortunate, yet someone else had endured far worse.

Setting down the page, he examined the unsent envelopes. They bore neither stamps nor addresses and had yellowed with age. He arranged them chronologically and opened the first, written twenty years earlier when the child was only two.

“Doctor Chen, this is the first time I’ve come across such a brilliant child. He picks up stuff at a superhuman rate.

“Born in a hidden corner of this institution and raised among the mentally ill—should I send him away?

“He will undoubtedly become a genius, but his reactions worry me.

“Since learning to speak, he has talked to himself like his mother. No—it feels as if he communicates with something invisible to us.

“The doctors and nurses are overwhelmed. No one except me has time to teach him language, yet I hear strange words from his lips. Did he overhear the staff, or is someone else teaching him?

“I have always been a materialist, but this child has shaken my certainty. People say infants can see what adults cannot. Could that be true?”
